items.title: Unify Separate: ‘Perfect Is Boring’ – Leo Josefsson on ‘The God Particle’
items.summary: Unify Separate's Leo Josefsson discusses "The God Particle," out November 6, 2026, technical perfectionism, AI and working with Richard Oakes of Suede.
items.fullText:
A Stockholm barbecue, a rather enthusiastic rendition of Glen Campbell’s “Rhinestone Cowboy” and an unexpected meeting between musicians from two different musical traditions: the beginnings of Unify Separate were hardly conventional. When Scottish vocalist Andrew Montgomery, formerly of Geneva, met Swedish producer Leo Josefsson in 2015, their contrasting artistic backgrounds became the foundation of a partnership that continues to evolve more than a decade later.

The Scottish-Swedish electronic duo’s forthcoming third album, “The God Particle”, is due on November 6, 2026, and introduces harder electronics and more assertive rhythms while confronting questions of mortality, political uncertainty, technological dependence and personal vulnerability. Andrew’s expressive vocal style remains central, but Leo’s increasingly elaborate production gives the new material a noticeably different physical presence. The album follows the single “Heart Aches”, released October 29, 2026.

Josefsson’s creative activities, however, extend considerably beyond Unify Separate. His history with Statemachine and LOWE, production work with Priest, collaborations with Rednex and Nassim Al Fakir, and increasingly extensive visual work for Diary of Dreams and The Mobile Homes reveal a musician whose interests have never been particularly obedient to genre boundaries.

In this conversation with Karo Kratochwil for Side-Line, Leo discusses the creative tension between his and Andrew’s musical backgrounds, the almost obsessive pursuit of technical perfection and his reservations about artificial intelligence. He also shares stories involving Richard Oakes of Suede, Adrian Hates, Priest and the unexpected rewards of simply having the courage to ask.

Interview with Leo Josefsson

Karo: Leo, the story of how you met Andrew Montgomery is rather wonderful: a barbecue in Stockholm, a spontaneous rendition of Glen Campbell’s “Rhinestone Cowboy,” and the beginning of a musical partnership. What did you hear in Andrew’s voice that made you immediately recognise its potential alongside your electronic compositions? And after more than a decade of working together, does he still manage to challenge your musical instincts?

Leo: Growing up with a lot of synthpop and various forms of electronic music shaped my musical identity in many ways. In my late teens, I also listened to a lot of indie pop, mainly from the UK, and Andrew’s former band Geneva was definitely on my radar.

When we met on that rather boozy night in 2015, we were taking a break from LOWE, and I was getting a little tired of my own vocals and being the frontman for so many years. I felt it would be nice to step back into the kind of role I’d had in Statemachine – behind the machines, taking on the occasional lead vocal.

I instantly felt that Andrew’s angelic voice would be incredibly interesting to explore. It was obvious that his voice complemented my darker presence, and the potentially fascinating combination of indie and synth immediately sparked production ideas.

And yes, working with a vocalist of Andrew’s calibre constantly challenges me to create the kind of soundscapes his voice deserves.

Karo: You came from the Swedish electronic scene with LOWE and Statemachine, while Andrew’s musical history takes us back to Geneva and the British indie scene of the 1990s. Those are two quite different traditions, particularly in their approaches to melody, emotional expression and production. Have you gradually developed a common musical language, or is the tension between those backgrounds precisely what keeps Unify Separate interesting?

Leo: That’s an interesting question. We both have very different musical (and cultural) backgrounds, and it’s incredibly liberating to see how well they come together when we’re writing music. There’s no ego involved, but our ambitions are always very high. Andrew’s melodies differ vastly from mine, and that clash can sometimes lead to really interesting results. So in a way, we’ve created a common musical language, but it’s constantly taking on new shapes. Or dialects, if you will. 🙂

Karo: “The God Particle” is a rather provocative title for an album concerned with human vulnerability, grief and existential uncertainty. You’ve described music as something that helps make sense of life’s contradictions. But can music actually provide answers, or does its real value lie in allowing us to confront questions that resist rational explanation? Has your understanding of what music can accomplish changed over the years?

Leo: I wouldn’t necessarily call “The God Particle” a provocative title, but perhaps a brave one. It tackles some very big subjects about existence and how we perceive life. I don’t think music necessarily provides answers, but it can help us navigate feelings and difficult times. Something that can “hold your hand” when you’re lost or simply need some perspective. It can also be incredibly powerful to listen to music you wouldn’t normally listen to. It can take you places and make you feel at home in the most unexpected surroundings.

I wouldn’t say my understanding of music’s impact has changed dramatically. It’s more that I’ve learnt so much about myself over the years that I now have a better understanding of the effect music has on me. How it can heal or distract. Soothe or impact. (Wow, that’s actually a pretty good lyric line!) 🙂

Karo: There’s a noticeable shift between “First Contact,” “Music Since Tomorrow” and the harder electronic direction of “The God Particle.” You’ve previously acknowledged that touring exposed a need for more dynamic material. How much of the new album was shaped by that physical experience of performing? Did you begin writing differently because of what you observed onstage, or did the live performances simply confirm an evolution already underway?

Leo: We’re incredibly fortunate to have had the opportunity to play so much in Germany, where we really feel a strong connection with the audience. That connection is very powerful. We give every last breath we have on stage, and in return, we receive so much energy from the audience. It’s an amazing exchange. We’ve definitely brought that energy back into the studio and into our songwriting. We feel very much at home with emotional synthpop, but we also really enjoy exploring more aggression and more direct arrangements. It feels like a natural step for us. It’s something that’s been there beneath the surface for quite some time, and now it’s finally coming out. And I think you might be surprised when you eventually hear some of the songs we’re already working on for the future.

Karo: The new album moves between collective anxieties and intensely personal emotions, with titles such as “Slow Armageddon,” “Kill the Machine,” “Heart Aches” and “Forever Chemicals.” Are you and Andrew increasingly interested in the relationship between private emotional life and the larger systems that shape it? And do you worry that apocalyptic imagery has become so familiar in electronic music that listeners risk becoming immune to its meaning?

Leo: Yes, I can definitely say we’re interested in both our personal lives and the bigger picture. I’m much more introverted when I write. I hardly read anything, neither books nor the news, whereas Andrew reads a lot. And I mean A LOT! His knowledge of history, politics and just about everything else is quite remarkable.

Andrew writes most of the lyrics, and I’m constantly amazed by how many layers they contain and how differently they can affect you depending on your mood when listening. I think our different perspectives sometimes create something that even we find astonishing.

Our apocalyptic imagery comes naturally to us, and we don’t really compare ourselves to what other bands are doing. The world is taking turns that we can barely keep up with, and we’re simply trying to find some beauty in all of it.

Karo: You’ve spoken quite openly about your pursuit of technical perfection, particularly during the making of “Music Since Tomorrow.” But technical sophistication and emotional impact aren’t necessarily the same thing. Has your understanding of a successful production changed? Do you ever find yourself deliberately resisting the temptation to improve something because its imperfections communicate more than a perfectly controlled arrangement could?

Leo: To answer this, I think I need to approach it from a slightly different perspective.

Growing up, I never really considered that I might have some kind of diagnosis that could explain certain aspects of my personality. And perhaps I don’t. But in recent years, it’s as if something has awakened in me. Part of that might be down to the pandemic. Another part probably comes with age, increased self-awareness and experience. I’m more emotionally driven than ever before. It’s almost as if I’ve been hiding a person inside me who’s now determined to come to the surface.

In everyday life, the perfectionist side of me is becoming quite ridiculous. When I load or empty the dishwasher, everything has to be in exactly the right place. When I choose a T-shirt in the morning, it has to feel 100% right. Sometimes I change several times before I’m satisfied.

And this mindset definitely carries over into the way I write, produce and mix music. I’ve invested thousands of hours in technical aspects of music production that probably aren’t particularly healthy, or even necessary! Many of these details aren’t even noticeable to the human ear. But I believe they can be felt. And knowing what I’ve put into creating and finishing a song makes an enormous difference to me personally. I don’t take shortcuts. (And I’m not talking about Command-Z here!) If creating a bassline means running it through several saturation boxes, plugins and effects pedals before recording it back through an amplifier to achieve exactly what I’m after, then that’s what I’ll do.

I practise something called hybrid mixing and top-down mixing, which means that, at an early stage, I run the mix bus through various pieces of hardware, compressors, EQs, saturators and colour boxes, as well as plugins. To make things even more “difficult,” I also use analogue summing and outboard inserts that affect how the mix sounds and feels. It’s a time-consuming process, and it certainly complicates things. But at the same time, it gets me to where I want the production to be. So yes, I want things to be perfect. But perfect is boring.

That’s why I always try to leave at least a couple of things slightly unpolished, unexpected or deliberately out of place.

Perhaps “Slow Armageddon” is a good example as well, or more noticeable than “Return to Exile” (?).

Karo: You’ve taken on a more prominent vocal role within Unify Separate, including songs such as “DETOX” and “Return to Exile.” You’ve described the human voice as another instrument, but surely singing also changes your relationship with a composition. Do you experience a different kind of vulnerability when performing your own material? And how do you and Andrew decide whose voice can communicate a particular emotional perspective most convincingly?

Leo: Yes, that’s true. The voice is often the most important instrument! This might sound strange, but I think that even applies to instrumental music. I believe that when you listen to music, your inner voice somehow resonates with the melodies and harmonies. That’s how you connect with the music, whether there are words or not. I think Andrew’s voice and mine complement each other, sometimes surprisingly well, and that’s a tremendous asset for Unify Separate.

More often than not, it’s obvious that Andrew’s voice outshines mine. But sometimes I can perhaps contribute a different emotional spectrum that completes the arrangement. And there’s definitely a certain vulnerability in stepping forward vocally, especially when you’re used to being the person behind the machines. But perhaps that’s also what makes it interesting.

Karo: Electronic musicians have always embraced technological innovation, yet you’ve expressed reservations about AI and automated creativity. What concerns you most: the potential disappearance of human authorship, the economic consequences for working musicians, or the possibility that artistic expression itself becomes increasingly standardised? And where do you personally draw the distinction between technology that expands creativity and technology that begins to replace it?

Leo: OK, here’s where I feel I have to take a stand and bring up something I find both important and quite interesting. Before AI, the creation of art and music was almost taken for granted. It was as if it had somehow lost some of its value, or at least suffered from a kind of inflation. Now that AI has entered the world of music creation, it’s almost as if “real music” can suddenly be appreciated in a different way. And I think that’s a good thing.

We’ll have to see what the long-term effects will be, but I’m quite confident that AI’s greatest potential lies in areas such as science, education, logistics and medicine. For me, the distinction is between technology that helps us express something and technology that tries to replace the person doing the expressing.

To truly connect with music, I believe the listener needs to feel a connection with real emotions, rooted in real human experiences. Not some cosmic meltdown of AI calculations and algorithms served up as music that a machine thinks we want to hear. And I think this distinction will become even more obvious when experiencing music live. Performed by humans. For humans.

Karo: Your relationship with Diary of Dreams has developed into something rather more interesting than the live collaborations many listeners already know about. You’ve recently been involved in the video for “my Vertigo,” and Adrian Hates publicly thanked you, Darkhall Filmstudio and Cthulhu Media, adding that you’d saved him. What exactly happened behind the scenes? How did you become involved in the band’s visual work, and how much creative freedom does Adrian give you when translating his musical universe into images?

Leo: We’re incredibly fortunate that Diary of Dreams have taken us under their wing and given us so many opportunities to support them live. That has opened quite a few doors for us, so a huge thank you to them and especially Adrian Hates for that!

Adrian and I have actually been talking for a long time about working together on visuals and music videos for Diary of Dreams. As for the “saving” part of his message, I think that mainly refers to the fact that, due to circumstances beyond our control, we had to postpone filming and production. At one point, meeting the deadlines seemed almost impossible. I tried to be as flexible as possible and worked incredibly hard within a very short timeframe to help bring his vision to life. So I imagine that’s at least part of what he was referring to.

I’m also involved in the video for “der Dunkelheit,” which premieres at 8 PM tonight (the very evening I’m answering these questions!) Adrian has a very clear vision of what he wants, but he’s also been extremely open to my ideas. We’ve been bouncing ideas back and forth until we both feel we’ve found the right approach. It’s a really rewarding creative process. I think “my Vertigo” turned out beautifully, with Adrian performing in a black-box studio environment that works incredibly well with the song.

For “der Dunkelheit,” the other song in the double release, we filmed Adrian in a similar setting, but also created a complementary storyline here in Stockholm. We cast Liv Östberg, who happens to be Richard Oakes’ stepdaughter (yes, Richard from Suede!) and she delivered an amazing performance.

It’s been a very rewarding experience, and I really enjoy being able to contribute to the visual world of Diary of Dreams.

Karo: You’ve also co-produced Priest’s “Altered State Police” with Linton Rubino and handled the album’s mixing. Priest already have a very distinctive sonic identity, so I’m curious about the negotiations that take place when another producer enters that creative environment. Where did your ideas genuinely change the direction of the record? And does producing another artist’s music sometimes offer greater freedom than working on your own compositions, where you’re inevitably attached to your original intentions?

Leo: Yes, this was a great honour for me! We actually talk about this in more depth in my podcast Under the Skin With… PRIEST, available on YouTube.

Linton and I connected when we played with Priest in Jönköping last year. I think we both realised very quickly that we should work together. Just a few weeks later, Linton came to my studio in Stockholm and played me some of the songs he was working on for “Altered State Police.” I loved everything I heard and immediately embraced his vision for the album. It was almost as if a circle of trust was formed right there and then. Linton had already done some really solid pre-production work, and it felt as though he was handing over his babies to me. I think he wanted me to treat the album with my somewhat unusual production techniques and, of course, have access to my synth collection and all my analogue gear. 🙂

So there weren’t really any negotiations. I took his productions, treated them with enormous respect and made them mine. Actually, not mine – ours!

I also had a very clear ambition that I wasn’t prepared to compromise on. I wanted the entire album to feel like a journey through sound and emotion, with all the songs fitting together as one coherent piece. I had a plan for how to achieve that. I experimented with lots of different audio chains, combining hardware and plugins, to find a sonic approach that would work across the entire album and make it feel like one entity.

Throughout the process, Linton was highly involved, giving feedback while also allowing me a tremendous amount of creative freedom. That trust was incredibly important to the final result. I don’t think we fundamentally changed the direction of the album. Rather, we allowed it to evolve into something that truly did the songs justice. Linton’s songwriting and the way he’s embraced his role as a singer are incredibly impressive.

I’m far too biased to evaluate my own contribution objectively, but I’m extremely proud of what we created together.

Karo: Your collaboration with Richard Oakes of Suede is particularly interesting given Andrew’s history with Geneva and Nude Records. His contributions to “The Void” and “Waiting Game” brought a different musical sensibility into Unify Separate. Did Richard fundamentally alter your original arrangements, or did he understand immediately what the compositions needed? And what distinguishes a meaningful artistic collaboration from simply inviting an accomplished musician to contribute to an existing recording?

Leo: This is actually a very inspiring story, and perhaps something others can learn from. Let’s call this little exercise “The question is free.” If there’s an opportunity, take it! (Am I Jesus? Hmm. My last name is after all Josefsson = son of Joseph!) Anyway…

We’d had the amazing opportunity to open for Suede in Stockholm, and in my world, that meant there should be something more to it than just the incredible experience itself. So I suggested to Andrew: “Why don’t we ask Richard if he’d like to play the guitar parts I’ve sketched out for The Void?” Andrew, being very British and polite, immediately said: “No, you can’t do that! He’s far too busy!” And I thought: “Well, yes, he probably is. But you never know…”

So I asked. And Richard was actually honoured! The stars aligned, we managed to find a date, and he came to my studio in Stockholm. We had a fantastic time recording together. I had to rub my eyes a couple of times because, hey: Richard Oakes is actually in my studio playing guitar for me!

The recording went really well, and Richard came up with ideas we would never have thought of ourselves. His contributions genuinely made a difference to the song. We still had a couple of hours to spare, and being rather shameless, I asked if he’d like to hear another song that was almost finished. That song was “Waiting Game.” He immediately picked up the guitar again and started playing. I pressed record. The rest is history.

Unfortunately, Andrew couldn’t be there that day, but I had quite a surprise waiting for him. Richard Oakes playing on not one, but TWO songs on the album! So yes, the question is free. The worst that can happen is that someone says no, perhaps even slaps you in the face with it. But at least you gave it a go!

Fun fact: The young girl’s voice you hear on “The Void” is actually my daughter Juno’s contribution. And yes, she was named after the synthesiser! 🙂

Karo: LOWE and Statemachine remain important chapters in your career, and LOWE’s recognition at the Scandinavian Alternative Music Awards belongs to a period when the Scandinavian synth scene had a rather different infrastructure. Looking at that scene today, what do you think has genuinely improved, and what has been lost? Has the disappearance of some of those older institutions made independent electronic music more fragmented, or has it opened opportunities that would once have been impossible?

Leo: I feel incredibly fortunate to have been part of this scene for so many years and to have played in two bands that mean the world to me. The places they’ve taken me and the people I’ve met along the way are things I’ll always treasure.

I’m not necessarily aware of every change that’s taken place, but it’s obvious that the way people consume music today is very different. There are so many new genres crossing over and sometimes helping the scene evolve. At the same time, I think it can all become a little confusing. Especially now that everything can be measured. There was a time when the number of CDs you sold at a gig could tell you something about your popularity. Now it often feels more like a competition of numbers and algorithms that nobody can really explain or fully understand.

I’m happy that some of the old record labels and distributors are still hanging in there. I feel quite nostalgic about that, and it’s something I find genuinely precious. I’m certainly not convinced that the synth scene is dying. But who knows what the next generation will choose to keep and cherish? And as you say, all these new possibilities also mean that people who might never have discovered the scene before can now find it and connect with it.

Viva la Synth!

Karo: Your work also extends to The Mobile Homes, a band with its own considerable history within Swedish electronic music. How does your approach change when working with artists whose aesthetic identity is already firmly established? Do you see production primarily as interpreting somebody else’s intentions, or should a producer sometimes be prepared to challenge the very qualities an artist considers central to their sound?

Leo: I grew up listening to The Mobile Homes and was a huge fan, so I feel like I know in my bones how they should sound. There’s never really been any conflict or complicated process in that respect. I’ve been involved in a few of their music productions, but even more so in their visual work. I’ve filmed and directed quite a few of their music videos (probably around ten by now!). It’s been incredibly rewarding to contribute to their visual identity and overall concept as well.

As a producer, I believe one of the most important things is to make the artist feel comfortable, relaxed and confident in what they’re doing. Your role is to get the very best out of their performance, listen carefully to their vision and, most importantly, truly understand it. And perhaps even amplify that vision.

Because at the end of the day, it’s their music and their legacy that matter most.

Karo: Your production work with Rednex, including the 2024 viral version of “Cotton Eye Joe,” offers an extraordinary contrast to the alternative electronic scene. You’ve also contributed to the Grammis-winning project by Nassim Al Fakir. Having experienced such different musical environments, do you think commercial success, cultural visibility and artistic achievement have become increasingly disconnected? And has witnessing the mechanics of viral success changed how you approach promoting Unify Separate, or made you even more sceptical of the industry?

Leo: This probably won’t go down particularly well in the synth scene, but hopefully there’ll still be a place for me after this interview. (Smiling nervously.)

I’ve actually been working with Rednex on and off since 2000. I hope that didn’t hurt the readers’ eyes too much! It’s been both a fun and challenging ride.

And working with my good friend Nassim Al Fakir, one of Sweden’s most popular public figures, and receiving a Grammis (the Swedish Grammy) has certainly strengthened my confidence.

I’m not a particularly sceptical person. I think that if you’re willing to explore different musical directions, there’s an enormous amount you can learn. It’s a bit like an actor who, at least once in their career, should crawl around on the floor barking like a dog, just to understand what that experience is like.

That’s why I’ve embraced so many different kinds of music, including commercial music. Sometimes to make a living, of course, but most importantly to learn, develop and evolve (and buy a lot of synthesizers!). I think commercial success and artistic achievement are two very different things. Sometimes they meet, sometimes they don’t. But there’s something valuable to learn from almost every musical environment.

Rather than making me feel disconnected, these experiences have given me a kind of bird’s-eye view of my own musical process. And I don’t think going viral is something you can really plan for. It’s often just a fluke that happens when you’re focusing on something else entirely.

Of course, I hope our music with Unify Separate will touch as many hearts and souls as possible. But I believe that takes hard work, determination and a little bit of luck. Although, if there’s some kind of music lottery I can enter, perhaps you could point me in the right direction? 🙂

Karo: Finally, with “The God Particle” approaching release, Unify Separate seem to be entering another particularly active period. Are you planning to take the new material further across Europe, and has the harder electronic direction changed your ambitions for the live presentation? Between Unify Separate, LOWE, your production work and now visual collaborations, you seem to have developed an unusually broad creative life. Is there still a musical direction you haven’t explored because you’ve never found the right circumstances, or perhaps the right person, to make it happen?

Leo: Yes, we’d absolutely love to play more shows across Europe, and we genuinely believe we’re a band that can deliver a great live performance at any level. Small club or arena. Andrew’s voice can knock just about anyone off their feet, and I think our music and visual presentation are incredibly powerful live. (What!? A Swede actually saying something positive about himself!?) We believe our harder direction and more varied live set have the potential to reach an even wider audience.

I’m amazed almost every day that I get to work creatively with so many talented people, whether it’s through music, visuals, photography or other creative areas. I’m always open to new collaborations, especially within the synth and electronic music scene. And as it happens, I’m currently involved in a project with one of Sweden’s biggest rock stars, so stay tuned for that!

But most importantly, check out our new album “The God Particle.”

And don’t be afraid to pick up the phone.

We’re coming for you!!

(Final word: don’t forget to buy more synthesizers!)

About Leo Josefsson

Leo Josefsson is a Swedish musician, songwriter, producer, mixing engineer and visual artist whose career reaches well beyond the boundaries of the electronic music scene in which he first established his reputation.

His early work with Statemachine placed him within Sweden’s developing synthpop movement, while LOWE provided an opportunity to explore a more expansive combination of electronic arrangements, melodic songwriting and live performance. As the band’s frontman, Josefsson contributed to albums including “Tenant,” “Kino International” and “Evolver.” LOWE and Statemachine received recognition at the Scandinavian Alternative Music Awards, helping establish his standing within Scandinavian electronic music.

Parallel to his activities as a performing musician, Josefsson developed an extensive career as a songwriter and producer. His credits include work with Rednex, Yaki-Da, Shebang and Daze, as well as collaborations across Swedish commercial pop. He worked with producer Oscar Holter within the Capitol Records/Universal environment, contributing to the development of artists including The Pusher, Alex Saidac and Robin Stjernberg. His songwriting and production credits also include “In My Head” by Tilly and Elliphant.

His work with Swedish musician and entertainer Nassim Al Fakir contributed to the Grammis-winning project “Årets Album.” These experiences reflect an unusually broad professional trajectory, ranging from underground electronic music to commercial pop, children’s music and international productions.

Josefsson’s contemporary production work includes collaborations with The Mobile Homes and Swedish electronic act Priest. On Priest’s 2026 album “Altered State Police,” he worked alongside Linton Rubino as co-producer and mixing engineer, helping shape the album’s overall sound through extensive experimentation with analogue equipment and digital processing.

His studio work has a particularly detailed approach to electronic sound design. Operating through his Stockholm-based Kiss the Needle studio, Josefsson combines analogue synthesizers, outboard equipment, saturation, hybrid mixing and digital production techniques. He has also taken responsibility for recording, producing, mixing and mastering Unify Separate’s albums, giving him considerable control over their sonic identity.

Alongside his recording career, Josefsson has developed an extensive body of visual work. He has directed music videos for The Mobile Homes and collaborated with Adrian Hates on the visual presentation of Diary of Dreams, including the 2026 videos for “my Vertigo” and “der Dunkelheit.” Photography, filmmaking, editing and visual storytelling have become important parts of his professional activities.

As a member of Unify Separate, Josefsson contributes synthesizers, programming, production, songwriting and vocals, working alongside Scottish singer Andrew Montgomery. The project provides a particularly interesting meeting point between his background in Swedish electronic music and Montgomery’s history in British indie rock.

About Unify Separate

Unify Separate is the Scottish-Swedish electronic duo formed by Andrew Montgomery and Leo Josefsson in Stockholm in 2015. Their collaboration brings together two distinct musical histories: Montgomery’s background as the frontman of British alternative band Geneva, whose releases on Nude Records attracted considerable attention during the 1990s, and Josefsson’s extensive involvement in Swedish synthpop through Statemachine and LOWE.

Initially performing under the name US, the pair released their debut album, “First Contact,” in 2019. Their second album, “Music Since Tomorrow,” originally appeared digitally in 2022, followed by a remastered CD edition in 2023. The record expanded their arrangements through guitars, more elaborate production and contributions from Suede guitarist Richard Oakes, who performed on “The Void” and “Waiting Game.”

Performances alongside Diary of Dreams, as well as appearances in Germany, Sweden and the United Kingdom, played a considerable role in the duo’s artistic development. Their 2025 “Heavy Meta” material introduced a harder electronic direction, subsequently expanded through remixes and further singles.

Their third studio album, “The God Particle,” scheduled for November 6, 2026, continues that evolution. Combining more forceful electronic production with Montgomery’s expressive vocals, the record examines personal loss, political uncertainty, technological anxiety and the search for meaning in an increasingly unpredictable world.

The duo’s music remains closely connected to their contrasting artistic backgrounds: Josefsson’s precise electronic construction and Montgomery’s melodic sensibility create a distinctive relationship between emotional immediacy and technical sophistication. More information is available on the duo’s official website.

items.title: Comfort Module releases new album ‘The Close’ on Lamour Records
items.summary: Swedish duo Comfort Module released its new album "The Close" on Lamour Records on October 23, 2026, following 2025 debut "Undertone."
items.fullText:
Swedish duo Comfort Module released its new album “The Close” on Lamour Records on October 23, 2026. The album pairs industrial EBM with alternative rock and electronic ballads.

“The Close” is available as a digital album and on CD, the latter in a DVD case limited to 150 copies. The tracklist runs:

  1. Driving
  2. End of the Rope
  3. My Only Friend
  4. I Am
  5. Broken
  6. Martyr
  7. Astray
  8. Setting Sun

The album was written, arranged and produced by Comfort Module. Pär Steen sings lead vocals, with additional vocals on “Driving” by Marie Steen and a choir on “My Only Friend” performed by Tusen Tungor, conducted by Linnéa Landström. It was recorded and mixed at Studio Soundrug and mastered by Joakim Westlund, with cover photography by Daniel Stigfelt and graphic design by rolfcarlwerner.

About Comfort Module

Pär Steen and Henrik Fexeus formed Comfort Module in Stockholm, Sweden, in 2025. Their debut album, “Undertone,” won the Synthsläggan award for Debut Album of the Year and was followed by two volumes of remixes featuring Agent Side Grinder, Rivet and Motormännen.

“The Close” is Comfort Module’s second album.

items.title: Obychno Odyn releases new album ‘Адинамия’ and video for ‘Погибель’
items.summary: Coldwave and post-punk project Obychno Odyn released the album "Адинамия" on October 30, 2026, with a video for its opening track, "Погибель."
items.fullText:
Coldwave and post-punk project Obychno Odyn released its new album “Адинамия” (“Adynamia”) on October 30, 2026, alongside an official video for the album’s opening track, “Погибель” (“Doom”).

The nine-track digital album is self-released. Its tracklist runs:

  1. Ненавистно
  2. Погибель
  3. Уходят люди и часы
  4. Мир угасает во тьме
  5. В никуда
  6. Холодная ночь
  7. Утро
  8. Lalala
  9. Жизнь пролетает нелепо

“Адинамия” is available as a digital album on Bandcamp.

About Obychno Odyn

Ukrainian musician Vadym Protsenko founded Obychno Odyn as a coldwave and post-punk project in 2025 in Bucharest, Romania. The project is now based in Turin, Italy. Bassist Marcello Aloisio joins Protsenko for live performances.

Obychno Odyn’s debut album, “Излияние” (“Outpouring”), followed on July 27, 2026, released digitally and on a 29-copy cassette edition with illustrations by Obychno Odyn. “Адинамия,” released October 30, 2026, is its follow-up, led by the single and video “Погибель.”

items.title: Ohms shares final single ‘Aeroplane Jelly’ ahead of debut album ‘Wechselströme’
items.summary: Melbourne post-punk act Ohms released "Aeroplane Jelly" on October 30, 2026, the last single before its debut album "Wechselströme".
items.fullText:
Melbourne post-punk act Ohms released its single “Aeroplane Jelly” on October 30, 2026. The digital track is the final single before Ohms’ debut album, “Wechselströme.”

All instrumentation and lyrics were written and performed by Lachlan P. Rother. The track was recorded and produced in a collaborative effort between Timothy Dunn, Andrew Robinson, Stuart MacKenzie and Rother, and mixed by Robinson and Rother. Mikey Young handled mastering.

Ohms also released an official video for “Aeroplane Jelly,” directed by Triana Hernandez and filmed in Peru, with camera work by Victor Torer and a performance by Calcio. The single’s artwork is taken from the video. Typography and design are by Sebastián Quintero.

“Aeroplane Jelly” is available as a digital single on Bandcamp.

About Ohms

Ohms is the Melbourne, Australia project of Lachlan P. Rother, formerly of U-Bahn and currently also a member of GLASNOST and High Control Group. Under the Ohms name, Rother has released a run of singles including “No Chance,” “Neon Violence,” “Declined (A Requiem For Human Services),” “Geworfenheit” and “Bimbo’s Inferno.”

“Aeroplane Jelly,” released October 30, 2026, is the final single before Ohms’ debut album, “Wechselströme.”

items.title: Suicide Commando x Assemblage 23 – I Am Your Darkness (Digital Single – Out Of Line Music)
items.summary: Side-Line contributor Karo Kratochwil reviews "I Am Your Darkness," the collaborative single by Suicide Commando and Assemblage 23 on Out Of Line Music.
items.fullText:
Belgian electro-industrial act Suicide Commando and US EBM project Assemblage 23 released the collaborative single “I Am Your Darkness” on October 30, 2026, via Out Of Line Music, pairing a radio edit with an extended “Kill Your Demons” version. Side-Line contributor Karo Kratochwil reviews the single below.

Forty years into Suicide Commando’s existence, Johan Van Roy has found an intriguing counterpart in Tom Shear of Assemblage 23. Their respective musical languages are instantly recognisable, although they approach intensity from different directions. Van Roy’s harsh, almost punitive vocal delivery and relentless electronic rhythms contrast with Shear’s more melodic, emotionally articulated approach. On “I Am Your Darkness,” these characteristics meet in a collaboration that makes considerably more sense than the stylistic differences might initially suggest.

The “Radio Edit” wastes little time establishing its intentions. The rhythm is fast, tightly programmed and characteristically uncompromising, while the synthesizers introduce a melodic urgency that has more in common with contemporary futurepop than traditional harsh electro. The vocals retain that familiar abrasive quality associated with Suicide Commando, yet the melodic construction carries a distinctly Assemblage 23 sensibility. The arrangement does not let one musical personality dominate the other; it preserves their differences. The resulting tension is precisely what gives the track its character.

The extended “Kill Your Demons” version develops the melodic side more fully. The electronic arrangements feel more expansive, with a sweeping, anthemic quality that contrasts rather effectively with the aggression of the vocals. Its forward momentum is practically irresistible, but the emotional register is more complicated than the rhythm initially suggests. There is an interesting ambiguity in transforming such difficult psychological material into music designed for collective movement. The dancefloor becomes a place where distress and exhilaration can occupy the same few minutes.

The collaboration is particularly successful because neither musician has attempted to disguise his musical identity. The familiar elements are all present, but their combination introduces a different balance between vocal aggression, melodic accessibility and rhythmic force. “I Am Your Darkness” is a convincing piece of contemporary electro-industrial music, direct enough to make an immediate impression and sufficiently well constructed to reward repeated listening.

Tracklist

  1. I Am Your Darkness (Radio Edit)
  2. I Am Your Darkness (Kill Your Demons)

About Suicide Commando

Founded in 1986, Suicide Commando has become one of the defining projects of European dark electro. Belgian musician Johan Van Roy has spent four decades developing a sound built around distorted vocals, confrontational lyrical subjects and meticulously programmed electronic aggression. From Critical Stage and Mindstrip to Axis of Evil and Goddestruktor, his recordings have helped establish a musical vocabulary that remains instantly identifiable. The new collaboration arrives during the project’s 40th anniversary year.

About Assemblage 23

Assemblage 23 is the long-running project of American musician Tom Shear, whose work occupies a fascinating intersection between electronic body music, synthpop and emotionally driven futurepop. Since the project’s beginnings in 1988, Shear has demonstrated a particular ability to combine muscular electronic arrangements with unusually personal songwriting. His 2025 album “Null” continued that trajectory.

Interestingly, this is not the first musical connection between the two projects. Assemblage 23 previously remixed Suicide Commando’s “One Nation Under God” in 2004 and “I’d Die for You” for the 2022 album Goddestruktor. “I Am Your Darkness” develops that existing artistic relationship into a direct collaboration. A five-track physical EP follows on December 3, 2026, with additional interpretations by DSTRTD SGNL, KLLSIGNL and J Wølf.

items.title: OH MADONNA – Obsession Nouvelle (Digital Single – Cold Transmission Music)
items.summary: Side-Line contributor Karo Kratochwil reviews "Obsession Nouvelle," the new single by OH MADONNA on Cold Transmission Music, released October 30.
items.fullText:
German darkwave/synth-pop duo OH MADONNA released the single “Obsession Nouvelle” on October 30, 2026, via Cold Transmission Music, following the duo’s debut single “Touch” on the same label. Side-Line contributor Karo Kratochwil reviews the single below.

OH MADONNA have an enviable understanding of how to make electronic music seductive without sacrificing its physical impact. Their latest single, “Obsession Nouvelle,” has that wonderfully immediate quality which cannot be manufactured through production alone. The rhythm is insistent, the synthesizers beautifully tempered, and the melody possesses an almost insolent ability to lodge itself in the listener’s memory.

The composition moves with confidence and a certain delicious irreverence. There is a cool, almost aristocratic elegance to its electronic arrangements, interrupted by a rhythmic urgency that refuses to let the music become too comfortable. The influence of ’80s synthpop is unmistakable, although the production has a contemporary sharpness, free from the excessive nostalgic sentimentality that sometimes plagues this particular musical territory.

Its greatest attraction lies in the songwriting. OH MADONNA understand that electronic sophistication means little without a memorable musical idea, and here they have several. The transitions are beautifully handled, the energy remains consistent, and the melodic structure has enough personality to make repeated listening a genuine pleasure. “Obsession Nouvelle” is a splendid little piece of dark electronic pop, intelligent in its construction and gloriously unconcerned with hiding its accessibility.

About OH MADONNA

Behind OH MADONNA are GEISTHA and nana del gray, two artists who met in Mannheim’s club scene and eventually brought their respective interests in music, visual art and literature into a shared project. Their collaboration is especially interesting because neither discipline appears subordinate to the other. The visual component belongs to the same artistic imagination as the music; it does not function as an elaborate accessory to it.

Their fascination with religious iconography, human desire and the contradictions of intimacy gives the project a wider cultural context, although the songs are perfectly capable of standing without that conceptual framework. And perhaps that is the crucial distinction. The imagery may invite interpretation, but the melodies do not require an explanation.

Cold Transmission Music deserves considerable credit for its discerning catalogue, and OH MADONNA are an excellent addition to it. With their debut album approaching, “Obsession Nouvelle” suggests that GEISTHA and nana del gray have a particularly rewarding musical partnership on their hands.

items.title: Lopsha shares video for ‘Basement Air’
items.summary: Lopsha has released "For Akira I" as a free Bandcamp download, including the video for "Basement Air," the album's opening track.
items.fullText:
Lopsha, the Adelaide, South Australia post-punk and darkwave project of Aleksei Prokhorov, has released “For Akira I” as a free download on Bandcamp. The album came out October 30, 2026, and opens with “Basement Air,” accompanied by the video for “Don’t stay blind.”

On YouTube the video carries the title “Don’t stay blind,” the line repeated through the track’s vocal. “Basement Air” runs 2 minutes 24 seconds. The video is a paper cut-out animation. It follows a family at home, each person absorbed in a separate routine, and a small girl who keeps praying with her eyes shut. Flashes of a hospital corridor cut into the scenes inside the house. A woman’s voice repeats the title line, “Don’t stay blind,” for the length of the track.

‘Basement Air’ opens Lopsha’s ‘For Akira I’

Prokhorov describes “For Akira I” as “written in the spirit of the Silent Hill 2 soundtrack.” He calls the album the first half of a two-part tribute to Akira Yamaoka, the composer of that soundtrack, and states that every song on it is an original composition. The eight-track, roughly 33-minute album is available as a free download through Bandcamp.

Tracklist

  1. Basement Air
  2. Sodium Light
  3. Negative Pressure
  4. Mercury Halo
  5. Concrete Bloom
  6. Nearer Elsewhere
  7. Dial Scar
  8. Bedside Zero

About Lopsha

Aleksei Prokhorov records solo under the name Lopsha from Adelaide, South Australia. His output spans classical guitar, ambient black metal, and darkwave and post-punk material. He writes, performs and records all of it himself.

Prokhorov’s catalogue traces back to a live acoustic concert billed as “Crystal Ship,” recorded in Tver, Russia, on 26 May 2010. He played guitar alongside Ilya Podoynitsyn on second guitar, flute and percussion, with Artem Sergeichev reading his own poetry and three Zambian musicians on percussion and backing vocals. Recordings from that night, including “Spring,” “Thunderstorm,” “Mustang” and “Koyunbaba IV” (the fourth movement of Carlo Domeniconi’s “Koyunbaba”), make up the 2026 album “Music of Open Doors.”

In 2026, Prokhorov released “Where Grief Goes Quiet” as Lopsha, a nine-track, 73-minute instrumental ambient black metal and drone album. Its track “Dormant,” an 8-minute 42-second instrumental, got its own official video, filmed at night from his car on the Fleurieu Peninsula, South Australia, on 22 September 2026.

“Basement Air” opens Prokhorov’s newest album as Lopsha, “For Akira I,” released October 30, 2026 as the first half of his two-part tribute to Akira Yamaoka, and offered as a free Bandcamp download.

items.title: Implant – I’m Only Happy When You Bleed (Digital EP – Alfa Matrix)
items.summary: The Belgian project Implant, led by Len Lemeire, has completed its fifteenth album. To announce...
items.fullText:
The Belgian project Implant, led by Len Lemeire, has completed its fifteenth album. To announce its arrival and whet fans’ appetites, the band has released the EP “I’m Only Happy When You Bleed”, featuring five tracks and three remixes.

Implant is a band that manages to avoid self-repetition while remaining distinctly recognizable. What strikes me about this EP is that the tracks are more subdued, each contributing to a particular atmosphere. It isn’t exactly ‘cinematic’, but rather feels like an experiment or a Freestyle Exercise, With Nods To EBM, Ambient, and Electro-Pop. Blend all these elements together, and you get a rough idea of what this EP is all about. Personally, I find that the tracks—especially the title track—lack a real climax. For me, the standout is “Pills (In F Sharp),” which has a slightly harder edge, a cool EBM-driven bassline, and a rich array of sounds and effects, all topped off by Len Lemeire’s vocals. I hate to say it, but the remixes—particularly those by Crash Course In Science, with their minimalist approach, People Theatre, with their vintage textures, and Aiboforcen—are all far more inspired than the original title track.

I’m used to a higher standard from Implant, but let’s wait for the full album before drawing any broader conclusions. (Rating:7).

Listen to “I’m Only Happy When You Bleed – Crash Course In Science Remix”:

About Implant

Implant is the electro-industrial project Len Lemeire started in Belgium in 1996. The debut CD single, “Fun,” credited to Lemeire alongside Geert Machtelinck, was pressed in a numbered edition of 1,000 copies that year. The project’s catalogue spans harsh EBM, industrial dance, electro-pop and dark synth across releases including “Implantology,” “Audio Blender,” “The Productive Citizen” and the EP “Fading Away,” closing most releases with the line “Did you have your Implant today?”

Implant released the free download single “The Drive” in December 2023. The twelfth studio album, “The Chaos Machines Part 1 – No More Flies On The Windscreen,” followed in May 2024. Lemeire discussed its modular-synth approach and a duet with Noemi Aurora in Implant interview: ‘Embrace chaos through the machines!’. The trilogy continued with the limited vinyl EP “The Chaos Machines Part 2 – Scratching The Surface” in September 2024 and closed with the album “Judging Sinners – The Chaos Machines Part 3” on February 7, 2025, again featuring Noemi Aurora and covered in Exclusive interview with Implant judging all those sinners.

“The Kinematics Of Doubt,” Implant’s fifteenth studio album, follows on October 30, 2026. “I’m Only Happy When You Bleed,” out now as an eight-track EP, is the second single revealed from the record.

Gloomy cold wave with powerful club energy

Right from the start, Nightsisters’ ‘All Things Must End’ exerts a power­ful pull. A juicy beat and a punchy bass drive the intro for­ward, whilst the dense, frosty cold wave sound cre­ates an intensely sombre atmosphere.

The deep, bari­tone vocals remind me of She Pleasures Herself, yet remain part of a mul­ti­fa­ceted vocal spec­trum. An urgent, uncom­prom­ising track that instantly cap­tiv­ates fans of atmo­spher­ic club clas­sics and cold wave.

items.title: “Just a Bad Dream” — Portland’s Masonique Confront a World of Surveillance and Political Absurdity in Video for “Too Many Villains”
items.summary: You are just a shadow A memory Just a bad dream Nothing to see Humanity has made a spectacular mess of its brief tenancy on Earth, and judging by the… The post “Just a Bad Dream” — Portland’s Masonique Confront a World of Surveillance and Political Absurdity i
items.fullText:
You are just a shadow
A memory
Just a bad dream
Nothing to see

Humanity has made a spectacular mess of its brief tenancy on Earth, and judging by the current crop of billionaires, bureaucrats, and technologically enhanced sociopaths, the eviction notice cannot come soon enough. We’ve got artificial intelligence rummaging through our private lives, politicians treating international diplomacy like a particularly vicious bar fight, and an American government increasingly fascinated by the architectural possibilities of incarceration. Somewhere amid this carnival of greed and institutional insanity, three musicians from Portland have decided that the appropriate response involves synthesizers, a bass guitar, and a healthy appreciation for human stupidity.

Masonique, the Portland post-punk outfit led by Ron Mason Gassaway, have returned with Too Many Villains, a wonderfully poisonous piece of electronic agitation and the first single from their forthcoming album, Otherhood, out October 30, 2026.

According to their gloriously ridiculous mythology, Masonique are time travelers dispatched to rehabilitate a ruined planet who accidentally landed during humanity’s continued existence. Consequently, they’re financing their escape by entertaining the very barbarians responsible for destroying civilization. Given the current state of affairs, their predicament seems increasingly plausible.

Musically, Too Many Villains occupies the wonderfully diseased intersection where Bauhaus meets Devo, with Gary Numan supplying the electrical paranoia and Mark E. Smith heckling everybody from a nearby pub. Keith Martinez’s monstrous bass line rolls through the arrangement with the determination of a bulldozer flattening government property, while Daniel Morris maintains a hypnotic, mechanically precise beat. Gassaway’s synthesizers introduce an atmosphere of technological derangement, alternating between abrasive electronic squalls and queasy melodic figures. His vocals carry the exasperation of a man watching civilization commit suicide through sheer administrative incompetence.

The accompanying video pushes the madness into outright hallucination. Bizarre, glitch-ridden animation carries us through distorted landscapes, brutalist prison architecture, flock cameras galore, and eventually the White House, where institutional authority acquires the visual characteristics of a particularly unpleasant fever dream. Faces and structures buckle beneath digital interference as the villains proliferate, poisoning every available corner of contemporary existence. There’s genuine anger beneath the absurdity, particularly when the song addresses algorithmic manipulation, arbitrary detention, manufactured wars, and the profitable destruction of the planet. Masonique turns that disgust into a relentlessly physical performance, allowing the music’s grotesque humor to sharpen its political accusations.

Watch the video for Too Many Villains below:

Too Many Villains preserves the recorded bass performance of Martinez, who died in December 2025. Desmond Cruz, now handling bass duties for the group, contributes backing vocals, connecting the present lineup with its predecessor.

Following 2024’s As The World Burns, Masonique sound thoroughly fed up with the species they’ve been condemned to entertain. Frankly, who could blame them? If the spaceship ever gets repaired, somebody should ask whether they’ve got room for a few passengers.

items.title: Seattle’s Ghosts In The Graveyard Summon a Séance Gone Wrong in Video for “Old Dark House”
items.summary: Dust on the banister, an unoccupied chair facing the door, footsteps from a room that should be empty: the old haunted house makes an accusation out of every ordinary object.… The post Seattle’s Ghosts In The Graveyard Summon a Séance Gone Wrong in Video for “
items.fullText:
Dust on the banister, an unoccupied chair facing the door, footsteps from a room that should be empty: the old haunted house makes an accusation out of every ordinary object. Domestic space becomes a kind of unfinished business, holding on to lives its current occupants never knew. Even before anyone calls a medium, there is the uncomfortable suspicion that the people paying the mortgage have mistaken themselves for the owners.

Seattle deathrock band Ghosts In The Graveyard give that suspicion a voice on Old Dark House: Resurrected Version. Taken from Monsters For The Masses: Resurrected, released October 23rd through Re:Mission Entertainment, the song sets a deep, resonant piano melody beneath Shelly Smith’s clear, ghostly vocals. Her delivery carries the formal poise of a Victorian ghost story, as though each line has travelled some considerable distance to reach the living.

Smith’s spectral presence and the song’s macabre elegance bring Mephisto Walz’s Mephisto Waltz to mind: both make gothic theatricality feel strangely intimate, drawing the listener close enough to become uneasy. Here, the piano gives that feeling a domestic setting, its measured notes suggesting an instrument being played somewhere else in the house.

Around a minute in, percussion begins to thump like unexplained banging in the attic. Colder electronic tones introduce Byron C. Miller’s distorted murmurs, with the rhythm growing rougher around him before Smith’s voice returns. As the piano comes forward again, Miller takes up a melody akin to hers, the two voices passing through one another until Smith closes the song. By then, the music seems to have acquired a second occupant.

Directed, photographed, and edited by bandmate Paul Morgan, the video turns this domestic disturbance into an affectionate homage to classic horror, with House on Haunted Hill among its touchstones. La Petite Mort and Miller play a troubled couple who call upon a psychic, portrayed by Tiffany Astrid, to investigate their unwelcome company. Megan Bishop appears as the Ghost Psychic, adding another presence to a gathering already short on reassurance.

The dining table becomes the centre of the trouble. Hands join, faces tighten in close-up, and translucent figures intrude upon rooms whose carved chairs and heavy curtains already seem prepared for their arrival. Smith’s production design gives the house its welcoming gloom, while Morgan’s superimpositions let faces and bodies occupy the same space with the peculiar wrongness of an old spirit photograph. A veiled figure at the table makes an ordinary seat look like a very poor place to sit.

Morgan approached the film with a clear affection for the methods behind those earlier hauntings:

“I shot it black and white to invoke the look of a classic horror film from the 1960’s, even though the video is not really set any one period. The idea of a seance gone wrong was intriguing to me, so I used that as jumping off point. We assembled a brilliant cast and they performed everything beautifully. I will stress that no AI or CGI was used in the making of this video. The ghost effects are all created using techniques that the horror filmmakers have used since the dawn of cinema.”

Watch the video for Old Dark House: Resurrected Version below:

The album surrounding Old Dark House: Resurrected Version has undergone its own return from the grave. For the tenth anniversary of their 2016 album, Ghosts In The Graveyard revisited the original recordings, with Morgan rebuilding the material through new production and programming, and Chris Longo mastering the new mixes. Reconstructed versions of Better In Black and Monster Mask sit alongside the collection’s sole newly added song, a cover of The Afghan Whigs’ Debonair.

For Miller, who began the project after eight years in God Module, the material reaches back further still. “The interludes on this album are made from cassette recordings I did when I was a little kid trying to be scary. In many ways these songs are the first half of my life as song.” Those childhood recordings give the reconstruction a personal charge: the adult musician is reopening rooms his younger self furnished with imaginary monsters.

items.title: Violet Oscillation Questions Faith and False Promises in Video for Dreamy Shoegaze Single “heaveness”
items.summary: Count all your blessings Write out a curse for all you have taken I’ll make your life worse Faith is a peculiar bargain when the people asking for it have… The post Violet Oscillation Questions Faith and False Promises in Video for Dreamy Shoegaze Single “heav
items.fullText:
Count all your blessings
Write out a curse
for all you have taken
I’ll make your life worse

Faith is a peculiar bargain when the people asking for it have already broken their promises. We are encouraged to count our blessings, accept inherited wisdom, and trust that those giving the orders know where they are taking us. Yet reassurance begins to sound rather sinister when it requires us to overlook what is plainly wrong. Once that trust gives way, doubt becomes difficult to contain. The search for meaning continues, complicated by the suspicion that those offering salvation have helped create the need for it.

That uneasy passage from belief to suspicion runs through heaveness, the new single from Thames Valley’s violet oscillation. Released October 30, it follows this year’s debut EP, it has become clear to me that all those who seek. The band’s frontman, Luca, has also become a familiar presence within shoegaze through Pedal Partners, his channel devoted to the effects and experiments that help turn six strings into something considerably less earthbound.

The song opens with small ripples of guitar and soft distortion, the reverbed strumming feeling almost like cool air against bare skin. Luca’s voice murmurs from the other side of the veil as the chords lengthen and the distortion gathers weight. My Bloody Valentine provides a reference for that friction between sweetness and abrasion, while Slowdive comes to mind in the suspended vocals and the sense of distance opening between each layer. The gradual swells suggest the patient, accumulating force of Explosions in the Sky, with post-rock scale meeting shoegaze’s intimate handling of the voice. Luca’s British inflections remain audible through the effects, a small human detail within all that amplification.

The lyrics read like an argument with people who claim the right to lead. Blessings turn to curses; sinners and preachers share the same uneasy company; promises of renewal run up against an older generation’s corruption. Luca moves between accusation, fear, and the suspicion that every available answer has already been compromised. There is a particular exhaustion in being told to read between lines that have themselves become suspect. By the closing admission, “i just think about it all the time,” the wider disillusionment has become a private, repetitive burden.

Luca says of the single: “This is my most poignant release to date, ‘heaveness’ is a visceral experience. Musically, lyrically & visually this is the most I’ve ever had to say.”

The accompanying video places Abstract in Sound’s twins within a landscape that seems unable to settle into a single version of itself. They walk along woodland paths and stand among the trees, their long hair and dark clothing giving the scenes a quietly gothic character. Violet and rose colour washes pass over the foliage; monochrome passages give way to bleached negative exposures, while overlapping images loosen the outlines of faces and branches.

Close-ups of a thorned stem interrupt the softer views of water and leaves, adding a sharp visual detail to the film’s diffuse light. The repeated images of the twins make recognition itself feel uncertain, as though the camera keeps returning to a memory it cannot quite recover. Its blurred surfaces suit the guitars, but there is also a useful connection to the words: amid so much visual transformation, even an ordinary path through the trees becomes difficult to trust.

items.title: “Where the Shadows Bend” — Cathedral Bells Cross into Another World With Haunting Dreampop Single “Put Me To Sleep”
items.summary: when I wake up again will it still be the same reality or just another dream There are mornings when the dream takes longer to leave than the person drifting… The post “Where the Shadows Bend” — Cathedral Bells Cross into Another World With Haunting Dreampop S
items.fullText:
when I wake up again
will it still be the same reality
or just another dream 

There are mornings when the dream takes longer to leave than the person drifting in it. We open our eyes certain that someone has just spoken, that a hand has rested beside ours, that a place we have never visited is somewhere we could find again. Falling asleep reverses that confusion: the room recedes while another world acquires its own unquestionable logic. At either end of the night, reality briefly loses its authority.

Each night, we submit to a small rehearsal for death, giving up our hold on the familiar and trusting that we will return. We cross into another world, meet its inhabitants, and accept its impossible arrangements. Hamlet’s fear of “what dreams may come” in the sleep of death troubles that same border: who can promise what awaits us once we have surrendered consciousness? Waking offers its usual reassurance, though the ache of a reunion that never happened can make the daylight feel considerably less convincing.

Cathedral Bells approach that uncertain crossing with their new single “Put Me To Sleep.” Led by Matt Messore and now based in Los Angeles, the band brings a tender physical warmth to questions about disappearance, memory, and whether the world will still be waiting when we open our eyes.

Soft drumbeats and gentle synthesizer tones open the song, leaving room for sustained guitar chords to spread around a delicate lead melody. Deep, warm bass gives the arrangement a reassuring weight beneath its suspended guitars. Messore’s singing is as soft as a down pillow, the words delivered with an intimacy that draws the listener closer. Classic 4AD-era dreamy post-punk provides a steady framework for the overlapping textures of dream pop and shoegaze; the layers gather around the voice without disturbing its quiet delivery. There is much here for admirers of Slowdive’s patient guitar work and The Radio Dept.’s hushed pop sensibility.

The lyrics ask whether waking will restore the same reality, and whether a loved one can still be remembered when the world loses its shape. A desire to escape the life we know carries the fear of losing our way back to one another. The repeated request to let go makes sleep an act of surrender, while something waiting beneath the ground brings the grave into view. Messore keeps these questions close to the body: the need to rest, the wish to remain beside someone, the uncertainty of what either person will remember on waking.

Listen to Put Me To Sleep below, and order the single here.

Cathedral Bells began in Florida in 2018, growing from Messore’s bedroom recordings into a touring band. Their self-titled 2019 EP preceded Velvet Spirit (2020), Ether (2021), and Everything At Once (2023). This April brought Parallel Dreams, their debut album for Artoffact Records, which introduced a more spacious approach and further slowcore influences. The band describes “Put Me To Sleep” as the beginning of a new chapter following their move to Los Angeles.

Following their October 29 appearance with Mind’s Eye and Tony Jupiter at the Roxy in Los Angeles, California, Cathedral Bells will support Alison’s Halo on a run of December dates through the western United States.
